extracted.intended_audience: students (undergraduate/graduate) and readers learning first-order logic and proof theory
extracted.subtask_description: Principles, algorithms, and axioms for parsing terms/formulas, definability/automorphisms, and a formal deductive calculus for first-order logic including axioms, substitution constraints, and modus ponens-based deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automorphism preserves definable relations (Corollary 22E)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let h be an automorphism of structure A, and let R be an n-ary relation on |A| definable in A. Then for any a1, ..., an in |A|, (a1, ..., an) ∈ R ⇔ (h(a1), ..., h(an)) ∈ R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: if ϕ defines R then |=A ϕ[[a1,...,an]] ⇔ |=A ϕ[[h(a1),...,h(an)]] by the homomorphism theorem. Use to show non-definability (examples: N is not definable in (R;<) because order-preserving automorphisms can map non-N points into N; length-one vectors not definable in vector-space structure because scalar-doubling is an automorphism that does not preserve length).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigidity of a structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A is rigid if the identity function is its only automorphism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A structure may or may not have nontrivial automorphisms; rigidity is a property used when arguing about what relations can or cannot be definable via symmetry/automorphism arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantifier-free formulas preserved by isomorphic embeddings
rubrics_metrics.description: If the identity map is an isomorphic embedding of (P;<P) into (N;<N), then for a function s: V → P and any quantifier-free ϕ, |=_(P;<P) ϕ[s] ⇔ |=_(N;<N) ϕ[s].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This equivalence can fail when ϕ contains quantifiers (example given where a universal sentence holds in P but not in N). Use caution: embeddings preserve quantifier-free satisfaction but not necessarily quantified formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definability from parameters (definable from points)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a fixed structure A, expand the language by adding a constant symbol ca for each a∈|A| to form A+. A relation R on |A| is definable from points in A iff R is definable in A+ (i.e., definable using those named elements as parameters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard notion of definability with parameters. Examples/guidance: finite unions of intervals with algebraic endpoints are definable in (R; +,·); real closed-ordered fields satisfy the first-order schema expressing least-upper-bound for definable-from-points sets, yielding decidability results (Tarski).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parsing terms: K function and parsing algorithm
rubrics_metrics.description: Define K on symbols by K(x)=1 for variables/constants and K(f)=1−n for an n-place function symbol f; extend to strings by summation. For any term t, K(t)=1 (Lemma 23A). Parsing algorithm: repeatedly split an expression using the first substring t with K(t)=1 to build the unique term tree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithm steps: (1) if all minimal vertices are single symbols (variables/constants) stop; (2) otherwise the first symbol must be an n-place function f; create n children and scan for leftmost t with K(t)=1 to label children; if first symbol not appropriate or no such t found, reject expression as non-term. Uniqueness follows from K properties and Corollary 23C.

rubrics_metrics.name: No proper initial segment of a term is a term (Corollary 23C)
rubrics_metrics.description: If t1 is a proper initial segment of a term t, then K(t1) < 1, hence t1 is not a term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence of Lemma 23B (terminal segments of a term are concatenations of terms) and K-additivity. Use this to argue uniqueness in parsing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parsing formulas: K function for formulas and unique readability
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend K to logical symbols (K(() = −1, K())=1, K(∀)=−1, K(¬)=0, K(→)=−1, K(P)=1−n, K(=)=−1). For any wff α, K(α)=1 (Lemma 23D); any proper initial segment α' of α has K(α')<1 (Lemma 23E), so no proper initial segment of a formula is itself a formula (Corollary 23F). Unique readability: wffs are freely generated from atomic formulas by E¬, E→ and Qi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parsing formulas uses same style algorithm as terms: identify atomic formulas or initial operator (∀ or '(') and split uniquely. Use K to locate correct splits; this justifies recursion definitions on formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for an expression to be a term (Jaskowski condition, Exercise)
rubrics_metrics.description: An expression ε consisting of variables, constants, and function symbols is a term iff K(ε)=1 and for every terminal segment ε' of ε we have K(ε')>0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stronger statement: if K(ε')>0 for every terminal segment ε' then ε is a concatenation of K(ε) terms. This provides an alternative effective test for termhood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a formal deduction (deductive sequence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A deduction of ϕ from Γ is a finite sequence α0,...,αn of formulas with αn=ϕ, where each αk is either in Γ∪Λ (Λ = logical axioms) or is obtained by modus ponens from earlier formulas (i.e., for some i,j<k, αj is αi→αk). If such exists, write Γ ⊢ ϕ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deductions are finite checkable sequences; theorems of Γ are precisely formulas obtainable from Γ∪Λ by finitely many modus ponens applications. Viewable equivalently as construction sequences or (conceptually) trees squashed to linear sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements of mathematical proofs/deductions
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof should be finitely long and effectively checkable; the set of proofs with empty hypotheses should be decidable/effectively enumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These requirements motivate the compactness theorem and enumerability theorem: compactness guarantees finite supporting subsets Γ0 ⊆ Γ when Γ ⊨ τ; enumerability ensures validities can be enumerated so 'proofs' (deductions) can be effectively found and checked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single rule of inference: Modus Ponens
rubrics_metrics.description: The chosen rule of inference is modus ponens: from α and α→β infer β.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All theorems are obtained from Γ∪Λ by repeated application of modus ponens. The deductive calculus presented uses an (infinite) axiom set Λ but only this single rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction principle for deductions (closure under modus ponens)
rubrics_metrics.description: If S is a set of wffs that includes Γ∪Λ and is closed under modus ponens (i.e., whenever α∈S and α→β∈S then β∈S), then S contains every theorem of Γ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this principle to prove that any proposed closed set containing axioms contains all deducible formulas; typical proof technique for soundness/completeness style arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical axioms: six groups (axiom schema)
rubrics_metrics.description: The logical axioms Λ are all generalizations of wffs of the following forms (where x,y variables and α,β wffs): (1) tautologies (from sentential logic using ¬ and →); (2) ∀x α → α[x:=t] (with substitutability restriction); (3) ∀x(α→β) → (∀xα → ∀xβ); (4) α → ∀x α when x is not free in α; and if equality included add (5) x = x; (6) x = y → (α → α[x↦y]) for atomic α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Axioms are included with all universal generalizations (∀-prefixes). Groups 1 and 2 require explanation: group 1 built from prime formulas and sentential tautologies; group 2 requires notion of substitutability to avoid variable capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitutability condition for substitution axiom (avoid variable capture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define 't is substitutable for x in α' recursively: (1) for atomic α always true; (2) preserved under ¬ and → (t substitutable for x in α→β iff substitutable in both α and β); (3) for ∀y α, t is substitutable for x iff either x does not occur free in ∀y α or y does not occur in t and t is substitutable for x in α.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Axiom schema ∀x α → α[x:=t] is included only when t is substitutable for x in α. Example hazard: substitution can cause capture (example where substituting y for x in ∀y Bx y produces an invalid axiom); exercise examples illustrate correct/incorrect instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tautologies as logical axioms (group 1) via prime formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: Axiom group 1 consists of generalizations of wffs obtainable from tautologies of sentential logic (using only ¬ and →) by taking the 'sentence symbols' to be the prime formulas of the first-order language (prime formulas = atomic formulas and those of the form ∀x α).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus verify a wff is a first-order tautology by treating prime formulas as propositional atoms and checking the corresponding sentential tautology. Example: (∀y ¬Py → ¬Px) → (Px → ¬∀y ¬Py) is such a tautology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-uniqueness of deductions (contrast with unique readability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike syntax-building (where terms/formulas have unique parse trees), a theorem does not have a unique deduction: there may be many different deduction sequences yielding the same formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is why the set of theorems is not 'freely generated' from axioms by modus ponens. Practical implication: proofs/deductions can be non-canonical; induction/closure arguments are used instead of uniqueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'generalization' and its role in axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: A wff ϕ is a generalization of ψ iff for some n ≥ 0 and variables x1,...,xn, ϕ = ∀x1 ··· ∀xn ψ. The logical axioms include all generalizations of certain schema-forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows axioms to be used with universal closure; when checking whether a particular universally-quantified axiom belongs to Λ, see if it is a generalization of one of the basic forms in the axiom groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using compactness and enumerability to obtain proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ ⊨ τ then by compactness there is a finite Γ0 ⊆ Γ with Γ0 ⊨ τ; hence σ0 → ... → σn → τ is valid for σi∈Γ0. By enumerating validities (enumerability theorem), one can eventually find that valid formula and verify its premises to produce a finite deduction proving τ from Γ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains how semantic consequence can be turned into a finite syntactic deduction using compactness plus an effective enumeration of valid formulas; motivates the deductive system design.
